exemplars.question: E1c
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil makes this a vivid opening by plunging us straight into Dido’s suffering and then letting us hear her own excited voice.
The book begins
at regina gravi iamdudum saucia cura
‘but the queen, long since wounded by a heavy care’
at marks an abrupt change of scene, and iamdudum places us in the middle of her suffering
with no build-up: her love has already taken hold before the book begins, and saucia, ‘wounded’, makes that love a physical injury.
This sudden start grips the reader at once.
vulnus alit venis et caeco carpitur igni
‘she feeds the wound in her veins and is consumed by a hidden fire’
Two metaphors, a wound and a fire, are set side by side, and the hard alliteration of c in caeco carpitur
makes the fire seem to bite at her. caeco, ‘hidden’, suggests she is keeping this love secret, and alit shows her nursing the very thing that hurts her,
so the opening image is vivid and already disturbing.
multa viri virtus animo multusque recursat gentis honos
‘the man’s great courage and the great honour of his race keep running back into her mind’
The repetition of multa … multus, the play on viri virtus and the frequentative recursat
show his qualities returning to her again and again.
haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque
‘his face and his words cling, fixed in her heart’
infixi is the language of a weapon driven in, and verbaque is enjambed into the next line,
so his words seem to cling on in the verse just as they do in her mind.
nec placidam membris dat cura quietem
‘nor does her care give her limbs peaceful rest’
completes the picture of a sleepless queen, with cura returning from the first line.
Virgil then pauses for a grand epic dawn:
postera Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras
‘the next dawn was lighting up the earth with Phoebus’ lamp’
The calm, bright light contrasts with her dark, restless night and makes the change to her speech more striking.
She speaks
male sana
‘hardly sane’
a blunt phrase which warns us that her mind is already unsettled.
Her first words are
Anna soror, quae me suspensam insomnia terrent!
‘Anna, my sister, what dreams terrify me and keep me in suspense!’
The switch into direct speech and the exclamation
bring us close to her fear and make her voice urgent and immediate.
quem sese ore ferens, quam forti pectore et armis!
‘how he carries himself in his looks, how brave in heart and arms!’
the breathless exclamations, quem … quam,
let us hear how dazzled she is, as if she can hardly finish a sentence.
The passage ends on two more exclamations,
heu, quibus ille iactatus fatis! quae bella exhausta canebat!
‘ah, by what fates he has been tossed! what wars he told of, endured to the end!’
so the opening closes at a high pitch of emotion, with Dido moved to pity for him.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). It engages with ‘vivid’ from the first sentence and follows the passage from narrative to Dido’s own speech. Quotations are well selected from every part of the passage and accurately translated. Features are precisely identified and their effects developed: the alliteration of c that makes the fire bite, infixi as the language of a weapon, and the enjambment of verbaque are all explained in relation to Dido’s state of mind, and the dawn is used well as a contrast. The final section is less developed: male sana is quoted but only briefly discussed, and the closing exclamations are identified without saying how they make the scene vivid. These small gaps keep it from full marks.

exemplars.question: E1c
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil makes the opening vivid by showing how much Dido is in love with Aeneas.
at regina gravi iamdudum saucia cura
‘but the queen, wounded for a long time by a heavy care’
uses a metaphor of a wound
to show that love is hurting her.
caeco carpitur igni
‘she is eaten by a blind fire’
is another metaphor, with alliteration of c,
which makes it more vivid.
segments.n: ‘More vivid’ could be said of anything. Say what the metaphor shows: carpitur, ‘she is eaten away’, makes love a slow, hidden fire consuming her from within, and caeco, ‘blind’, means no one can see it.

segments.t: Virgil then tells us that she keeps thinking about Aeneas’ courage and his family, and that she cannot sleep at night because of her love. The next morning comes and she goes to speak to her sister Anna.
segments.n: This paraphrases lines 3 to 8 and passes over rich Latin: haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque, ‘his face and words cling fixed in her heart’, extends the wound imagery, and the grand dawn of Phoebea lampade contrasts with the restless queen, male sana.

segments.t: haerent infixi pectore vultus
‘his face sticks, fixed in her heart’
shows that she cannot stop thinking about what he looks like,
which is a vivid way to show her love.
Dido speaks in direct speech,
which makes it more dramatic because we hear her own words.
She says
quis novus hic nostris successit sedibus hospes
‘who is this new guest who has come to our home?’
which is a question
showing that she is excited about him.
credo equidem, nec vana fides, genus esse deorum
‘I believe, and it is not an empty belief, that he is from the race of the gods’
shows that she thinks Aeneas is almost divine.

Dido then speaks to Anna and tells her that she has had terrible dreams, and that a new guest has come to their home. She says he is very handsome and brave, and that he must be descended from the gods.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 9 to 12. The exclamations quis novus hic … hospes and quam forti pectore et armis show Dido’s breathless excitement in her own words, which is exactly what makes the opening vivid.

segments.t: This shows that Dido has completely forgotten her dead husband Sychaeus, to whom she swore to stay loyal, which is why her love is a kind of guilt.
segments.n: Sychaeus is not mentioned in these lines, so this drifts from the passage and from the key word ‘vivid’.

segments.t: The word insomnia
is effective because it shows she cannot sleep.
segments.n: In quae me suspensam insomnia terrent, insomnia means ‘dreams’; the effect worth explaining is that her love torments her even at night and leaves her suspensam, ‘in suspense’.

segments.t: Overall the opening is vivid because we see Dido’s love from the start.

exemplars.commentary: This is a reasonable response at the top of Level 3. It engages with the question and makes some relevant points, supported by accurate quotation and translation. The metaphor of the wound and the image of Aeneas’ face fixed in her heart are sensibly explained. Development is limited elsewhere: the alliteration of c is said only to make the line ‘more vivid’, insomnia is taken to mean sleeplessness when it means ‘dreams’, and the remark that direct speech is dramatic could apply to any passage. Two paragraphs narrate the passage without analysis, so the repetition of multa … multus, the enjambment of verbaque, the contrast with the bright dawn and Dido’s excited exclamations are missed, and a point about Sychaeus drifts outside the lines set. The conclusion is tenable but simply repeats the opening.

exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil makes this a vivid opening to Book 4 because it is about Dido falling in love with Aeneas, which is the main story of the book.

In Book 1 Venus sent Cupid disguised as Ascanius to make Dido fall in love with Aeneas, and at the end of the book Dido asked Aeneas to tell the story of the fall of Troy, which he does in Books 2 and 3. So by the start of Book 4 she has been listening to him all night and is now in love.
segments.n: All of this happens before the passage begins. It may explain why Dido is in love, but it says nothing about how Virgil makes these fourteen lines vivid.

segments.t: At the start of Book 4 Dido is in love with Aeneas. She is wounded and she cannot sleep because she keeps thinking about him. She thinks about how brave he is and about his family, and she remembers his face and his words.
segments.n: A summary of lines 1 to 5 with no Latin. The wound is there to analyse: gravi iamdudum saucia cura, ‘long since wounded by a heavy care’, and vulnus alit venis, ‘she feeds the wound in her veins’, present love as an injury she keeps alive.

segments.t: Dido is a very emotional character throughout the Aeneid, and this shows that she is a tragic heroine like the ones in Greek tragedy.
segments.n: A general claim about Dido across the whole poem. The question needs evidence from these lines showing how the opening is made vivid.

igni
segments.n: igni alone only tells us there is fire. Quoting caeco carpitur igni, ‘she is consumed by a blind fire’, brings in the hidden, slow-burning nature of her love and the alliteration of c.

segments.t: This is very effective and makes the opening vivid.
segments.n: ‘Very effective’ and ‘vivid’ repeat the question without showing how. The answer needs to say what the image makes us see or feel.

segments.t: vulnus
segments.n: Another single word. vulnus alit venis, ‘she feeds the wound in her veins’, is the phrase that carries the point: Dido keeps her own wound alive.

segments.n: ‘Emphasises that she is in love’ says nothing about this metaphor. A wound she feeds herself suggests a love that is harmful and self-inflicted.

segments.t: In the morning she talks to her sister Anna and tells her about her dreams. She says that Aeneas is very brave and that he must be the son of a god.
segments.n: This retells lines 6 to 12. The vivid detail is in the Latin: the exclamations quis novus hic … hospes and quam forti pectore et armis capture Dido’s breathless admiration in her own words.

segments.n: arguit here means ‘proves’ or ‘reveals’: fear exposes low-born spirits, so Aeneas’ fearlessness proves his divine birth. Read as ‘argues’, the line loses Dido’s reasoning about why he must be a god’s son.

segments.n: This point grows out of the mistranslation. Dido is reasoning that Aeneas’ courage proves his noble birth, which shows how dazzled she is by him.

segments.t: She also says that he has been tossed about by the fates and that he told her about all the wars he fought in.
segments.n: A paraphrase of lines 13 to 14. The exclamations heu, quibus ille iactatus fatis! and quae bella exhausta canebat! show Dido’s emotion breaking into her speech, which is what makes it vivid.
