segments.n: The escape from Troy is told in Book 2 and is not in this passage. It does not help to show how Virgil makes this opening vivid.

segments.t: In conclusion, Virgil makes this a vivid opening to Book 4 because Dido is in love with Aeneas and she cannot sleep, and she talks to Anna about him. It is vivid because it shows how she feels.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the bottom of the level. It is a reasonable length, but most of it is narrative paraphrase of the passage or background from Books 1 and 2, which gains no credit. Only one Latin phrase is quoted, and degeneres animos timor arguit is mistranslated: arguit means ‘proves’, so the point built on it (that Dido is arguing with herself) is wrong. igni and vulnus are picked out as single words and called metaphors without any explanation of their effect, and ‘very effective’ is not development. The conclusion restates the question. To improve, the answer needed to quote whole phrases such as caeco carpitur igni and explain what they show about Dido’s love.

exemplars.question: E3a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil makes Anna’s arguments persuasive by combining affection with hard-headed reasoning, so that she appeals both to Dido’s heart and to her duty as queen.
She begins
o luce magis dilecta sorori
‘o you who are dearer to your sister than the light’
This hyperbole
shows how much she loves Dido, which makes Dido more likely to listen, because the advice clearly comes from love.
solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa
‘will you be worn away, alone and grieving, all through your youth?’
The rhetorical question, with sola placed first,
stresses Dido’s loneliness, and perpetua … iuventa, spread across the line, makes the waste of her youth seem endless.
nec dulces natos Veneris nec praemia noris?
‘and will you not know sweet children, nor the rewards of love?’
The repeated nec
lists the things she is giving up, and dulces makes them attractive,
so Anna appeals to Dido’s feelings.
id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos?
‘do you think that ashes or buried spirits care about that?’
This blunt question reduces Sychaeus to cinerem, mere ashes, and so undercuts Dido’s loyalty to him.
placitone etiam pugnabis amori?
‘will you fight even against a love that pleases you?’
The verb pugnabis is a military metaphor
which makes Dido’s resistance sound like a war against herself, and placito reminds her that she actually wants this love.
This is the turning point of Anna’s argument.
She then moves to politics with the anaphora of hinc:
hinc Gaetulae urbes, genus insuperabile bello
‘on one side the cities of the Gaetulians, a race unconquerable in war’
The list of fierce neighbours, the unbridled Numidians and the raging Barcaeans, makes Carthage seem surrounded, so marriage to a warrior looks like common sense.
Finally she uses praeteritio,
quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam germanique minas?
‘why should I mention the wars rising from Tyre and your brother’s threats?’
pretending not to mention the danger from Tyre while in fact ending on it.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response at the top of Level 4. It engages well with ‘persuasive’ and sees the two strands of Anna’s appeal, to feeling and to politics. Quotations are well chosen and accurately translated, and the rhetorical questions, the reduction of Sychaeus to ashes and the military metaphor in pugnabis are all well explained. Some points are less developed: the hyperbole point is fairly general, the political section summarises more than it analyses, and praeteritio is identified without drawing out the force of germani, a threat from Dido’s own brother. The concession esto and the list of rejected suitors (non Libyae, non ante Tyro) are not discussed, and there is no conclusion. Fuller development throughout would lift this into Level 5.

exemplars.question: E3a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Anna’s arguments are persuasive because she uses lots of rhetorical questions.
o luce magis dilecta sorori
‘o you who are dearer to your sister than the light’
shows that Anna loves Dido,
which makes Dido trust her.
segments.n: Develop it: by opening with this affectionate address, Anna wins Dido’s goodwill before she argues, so her advice sounds like love and gains force.

segments.t: solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa
‘will you be worn away alone, grieving for your whole youth?’
is a rhetorical question
which makes Dido think about how lonely she will be.
Anna then says that Dido will not have children, and that the dead do not care what she does. She reminds her that she has turned down Iarbas and the other African leaders.
segments.n: This skips some of Anna’s most persuasive lines. id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos? dismisses Sychaeus as mere ‘ash’ and buried shades, and the concessive esto grants Dido’s past refusals only to brush them aside.

segments.t: despectus Iarbas
‘Iarbas was despised’
shows that Dido has rejected other men before.
placitone etiam pugnabis amori?
‘will you fight against a love that pleases you?’
is another rhetorical question
that makes Dido realise that she wants to love Aeneas.
esto: aegram nulli quondam flexere mariti
‘granted: no husbands moved you once when you were grieving’
is a concession
which makes Anna sound fair.
segments.n: A start. esto, ‘so be it’, grants Dido’s past refusals only to brush them aside, so Anna seems reasonable while still pressing her case, and aegram reminds Dido how sick with grief she has been.

segments.t: Anna uses anaphora of hinc
to list the enemies around Carthage.
segments.n: The anaphora of hinc … hinc does more than list: it points first one way, then another, so Carthage seems hemmed in on every side, which makes a protector like Aeneas seem necessary.

segments.t: Numidae infreni
‘the unbridled Numidians’
sound dangerous, which would worry Dido,
so this is persuasive.
Anna then lists more peoples, the Barcaei and the desert region, and mentions the threats of Dido’s brother from Tyre.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 42 to 44. The praeteritio quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam germanique minas?, ‘why should I speak of wars rising from Tyre and our brother’s threats?’, mentions the danger while claiming to pass over it, a clever persuasive move.

segments.t: Dido’s brother Pygmalion murdered her husband Sychaeus for his gold, and Dido escaped with the treasure and some followers to Africa, where she bought land and founded Carthage.
segments.n: This story belongs to Book 1. Anna only hints at it here, and the point should be how the hint persuades.

segments.t: So Anna makes Dido feel unsafe, which is persuasive.
Anna is a good sister to Dido, and the reader feels sorry for Dido because later in the book she dies, which shows that Anna’s advice was wrong.
segments.n: What happens later in the book does not show how Anna’s words persuade here. Every point should explain how the language of lines 31 to 44 makes her case convincing.

segments.t: Overall Anna’s arguments are persuasive because she uses rhetorical questions and talks about the dangers around Carthage, which would make Dido want to marry Aeneas.

exemplars.commentary: This is a reasonable response in the middle of Level 3. It engages with the question and supports some points with accurate quotation and translation. Rhetorical questions are correctly identified, but their effect is described in general terms each time, and the concession esto is named with only a brief comment. Two paragraphs retell the passage and pass over much of Anna’s most persuasive material, such as the blunt reduction of Sychaeus to cinerem and the praeteritio about her brother. The anaphora of hinc is named without saying how it makes Carthage seem surrounded. The story of Pygmalion and the final paragraph on later events move away from the passage and gain no credit.

exemplars.question: E3a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Anna’s arguments are persuasive because she is Dido’s sister and Dido trusts her.

Anna is a very important character in Book 4. She is the only person Dido can talk to, and later she builds the pyre for Dido without knowing what it is for, and at the end she finds Dido dying and is very upset.
segments.n: Anna’s later role is outside the passage. The question asks how her words in lines 31 to 44 persuade, which needs her language.

segments.t: Anna tells Dido that she should marry Aeneas. She says that Dido is too young to be alone and that she should have children.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 32 to 33. The Latin carries the persuasion: solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa is a rhetorical question, and the emotive dulces natos, ‘sweet children’, appeals to what Dido is missing.

segments.t: Veneris
segments.n: One word picked out because it is easy to recognise. In context nec dulces natos Veneris nec praemia noris, ‘will you not know sweet children nor the rewards of love?’, is the argument worth analysing.

segments.t: is Venus,
the goddess of love, who is Aeneas’ mother, so this shows Venus is helping Aeneas.
segments.n: Here Veneris simply means ‘of love’, as in the rewards of love; Anna is not referring to the goddess helping Aeneas. The point drifts from how Anna’s argument persuades Dido.

segments.t: Then Anna says that the dead do not care about what Dido does, and that Dido has already turned down lots of men, like Iarbas and other African kings.
segments.n: This skips the sharpest Latin: id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos? reduces Sychaeus to ‘ash’ and buried shades, and the concessive esto grants Dido’s past refusals only to brush them aside.

segments.t: Iarbas is a king who later prays to Jupiter because he is angry that Dido has rejected him and chosen Aeneas, and this is why Jupiter sends Mercury to tell Aeneas to leave.
segments.n: Iarbas’ prayer comes later in the book. Here despectus Iarbas, ‘Iarbas scorned’, matters only as part of Anna’s case, and that is what needs discussing.

segments.t: Anna also says that there are lots of enemies around Carthage, like the Gaetulians and the Numidians, and that her brother is threatening her.
segments.n: A list of names from lines 40 to 44 without analysis. The descriptions make the threat vivid: genus insuperabile bello, Numidae infreni, furentes Barcaei, and the praeteritio quid … dicam germanique minas? mentions her brother while claiming not to.

segments.t: bello
segments.n: A single word, and one easily confused. The phrase genus insuperabile bello, ‘a race unconquerable in war’, is what makes the Gaetulians frightening.

segments.t: means
‘beautiful’
segments.n: bello is the ablative of bellum, ‘war’, here ‘in war’; it is not bellus, ‘beautiful’. The mistake reverses Anna’s point, which is that the neighbours are dangerous.

segments.t: so the Gaetulians are a beautiful race, which shows that Africa is a nice place to live.
segments.n: This conclusion comes from the mistranslation and is the opposite of Anna’s argument: she paints Carthage as surrounded by dangerous peoples so that Dido will want Aeneas’ protection.

segments.t: Dido’s brother is Pygmalion, who killed her husband Sychaeus, so Dido had to run away from Tyre and found Carthage.
segments.n: This story is told in Book 1. Anna only hints at it with germanique minas, and the answer should explain how that hint persuades.

segments.t: This makes the argument persuasive because Dido is scared.
Anna also asks Dido if she will fight against a love that pleases her, and reminds her where she is living, among dangerous tribes and next to the desert.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 38 to 39. placitone etiam pugnabis amori?, ‘will you fight even against a love that pleases you?’, is a pointed rhetorical question that turns Dido’s resistance into a fight against herself.

segments.t: She uses lots of questions to make Dido think, which is persuasive.
segments.n: The questions are neither quoted nor named as rhetorical questions, and ‘make Dido think’ does not explain how each one pushes her towards Aeneas.

segments.t: In the end Dido is persuaded and she goes to the temples to make sacrifices, hoping the gods will approve.
segments.n: What Dido does next is outside the passage and does not show how Anna’s words persuade.

segments.t: Anna’s arguments are persuasive because Dido is already in love with Aeneas, so she wants to be persuaded. Anna is a good sister, but her advice turns out to be bad because it leads to Dido’s death.
segments.n: The outcome of the book and Dido’s state of mind are not the same as Anna’s methods. The question asks how Virgil makes her arguments persuasive, which means looking at her questions, appeals and images.

segments.t: Overall Anna is persuasive because she gives lots of reasons.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very limited response (Level 1), at the top of the level. It is a reasonable length, but almost all of it is narrative paraphrase or background from elsewhere in the poem (Anna’s later role, Iarbas’ prayer, Pygmalion), none of which explains how Anna persuades. No Latin phrase is quoted; Veneris and bello are picked out as single words, Veneris is misread as a reference to the goddess, and bello is mistranslated as ‘beautiful’, which leads to a conclusion that reverses Anna’s argument. There is no discussion of her rhetorical questions, her emotive language or the anaphora of hinc. The final sentence asserts that she gives ‘lots of reasons’ without examining any.

exemplars.question: E7a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil presents Juno as cunning by showing her watching and waiting for her moment, and as persuasive through a speech that mixes sarcasm with apparent reasonableness.
The passage opens with the halted city:
non coeptae adsurgunt turres, non arma iuventus exercet
‘the towers that were begun do not rise, the young men do not practise arms’
The anaphora of non
lists everything that has stopped,
and
murorum ingentes aequataque machina caelo
‘the huge walls and the crane that reached the sky’
opens with three heavy spondees,
so the rhythm itself seems to stand still.
This is the weakness Juno sees and exploits: Carthage is defenceless while its queen is in love.
quam simul ac tali persensit peste teneri
‘as soon as she perceived that Dido was held by such a plague’
persensit, ‘perceived clearly’, and the word pestis
show Juno watching closely and judging Dido’s love as a disease, and
nec famam obstare furori
shows her noting that reputation no longer holds Dido back. She waits for the right moment, which is the mark of a cunning schemer.
talibus adgreditur Venerem Saturnia dictis
‘with such words the daughter of Saturn approaches Venus’
adgreditur can mean ‘attack’,
so her speech is presented as an assault, and the title Saturnia reminds us of her grand and dangerous ancestry.
egregiam vero laudem et spolia ampla refertis
‘truly it is outstanding glory and rich spoils that you are winning’
This is sarcasm, using the language of a military triumph,
which mocks Venus’ victory over a woman as if it were a great conquest. By starting with mockery Juno puts Venus on the defensive,
a cunning way to begin a negotiation.
The parenthesis
tuque puerque tuus magnum et memorabile numen
‘you and your boy, a great and memorable divine power’
continues the sneer with mock-epic grandeur.
una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est
‘if one woman has been defeated by the trickery of two gods’
una and duorum frame the line, and dolo divum alliterates,
stressing how unequal the fight was: two gods against one woman. Juno makes Venus’ victory sound shameful,
which pressures her to agree.
sed quis erit modus, aut quo nunc certamine tanto?
‘but what limit will there be, or where are we going now with so great a contest?’
The closing rhetorical questions
make Juno sound tired of quarrelling and reasonable, which prepares for her offer.
Having attacked, she now seems to make peace: a persuasive change of tone.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response at the bottom of Level 5. It engages with both parts of the question, cunning and persuasive, and uses the opening lines intelligently as the situation Juno exploits; the observation about the spondees is accurate and relevant. The sarcasm, the mock-epic parenthesis and the framing of the line by una and duorum are well explained and linked to the question. Some points could be developed further: nec famam obstare furori is quoted without translation, the point about Saturnia is asserted, and the lines in which Juno shows she understands Venus’ fears (nec me adeo fallit …) are left out, though they would strengthen the case for her shrewdness.

exemplars.question: E7a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Juno is presented as cunning and persuasive in the way she speaks to Venus.
At the start of the passage the building of Carthage has stopped because Dido is in love, and the young men are not training.
segments.n: This summarises lines 86 to 89 without the Latin. The anaphora of non and the image of pendent opera interrupta, ‘the works hang broken off’, show the damage Juno is reacting to, which sets up her move.

segments.t: quam simul ac tali persensit peste teneri
‘as soon as she realised that she was held by such a plague’
shows that Juno thinks Dido’s love is a disease, and she is waiting for her chance.
egregiam vero laudem et spolia ampla refertis
‘you are bringing back outstanding praise and great spoils’
is sarcastic
because Juno does not really think that defeating Dido is glorious. She is mocking Venus,
which is cunning because it makes Venus feel embarrassed.
tuque puerque tuus
‘you and your boy’
refers to Cupid in a mocking way, as if he is just a child.
una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est
‘if one woman has been beaten by the trick of two gods’
contrasts one and two,
which shows that it was an unfair fight, so Venus should be ashamed.
Juno is also persuasive because she uses sarcasm again when she calls Venus and Cupid magnum et memorabile numen.
This is sarcastic, which shows she is mocking them.
segments.n: This repeats the earlier sarcasm point without developing it. The mock-epic grandeur of magnum et memorabile, ‘great and memorable’, applied to two gods who have beaten one woman, is what makes the jibe bite.

segments.t: Juno has always hated the Trojans and loves Carthage, so it is not surprising that she wants to stop Aeneas from leaving. She knows that Rome will one day destroy Carthage.
segments.n: Juno’s motive comes from outside the passage. The question asks how she is presented as cunning and persuasive in these lines.

segments.t: nec me adeo fallit veritam te moenia nostra suspectas habuisse domos Karthaginis altae
‘it does not escape me that you, fearing our walls, have held the homes of high Carthage under suspicion’
shows that Juno knows what Venus is thinking, which makes her seem clever.
sed quis erit modus
‘but what will be the limit?’
is a rhetorical question
which makes her more persuasive.
segments.n: Say how. sed quis erit modus, ‘but what will be the limit?’, makes Juno sound reasonable, as if she wants to end a quarrel, which disguises the scheme she is about to propose.

segments.t: Overall Virgil presents Juno as cunning because she flatters and mocks Venus at the same time, and as persuasive because she sounds reasonable.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response at the bottom of Level 4. It engages with the question and covers Juno’s speech with accurate quotation and translation. The sarcasm of egregiam vero laudem is explained, and the contrast between one woman and two gods is developed well. The opening lines are only narrated, so the paralysis of the city is not linked to Juno’s scheming, and the language of attack in adgreditur is missed. magnum et memorabile numen is noticed, but the answer only repeats that it is sarcastic, and a paragraph on Juno’s hatred of the Trojans brings in material from outside the passage. The final rhetorical question is identified without any explanation of how it persuades.

exemplars.question: E7a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Juno is cunning because she makes a plan to trick Venus.

Juno is the queen of the gods and the wife of Jupiter, and she hates the Trojans because of the judgement of Paris, when Paris said Venus was more beautiful than her. She also loves Carthage, so she does not want Aeneas to reach Italy and found the Roman race, which will one day destroy Carthage.
segments.n: This comes from outside the passage and explains her motive. The question asks how Virgil presents her as cunning and persuasive in these lines, which needs evidence from her speech.

segments.t: At the start of the passage the building of Carthage has stopped because Dido is in love. The towers are not rising, the young men are not training with weapons and the walls are left unfinished.
segments.n: This summarises lines 86 to 89 without the Latin. The anaphora of non and the image of pendent opera interrupta, ‘the works hang broken off’, show the damage Juno is reacting to, which sets up her move.

segments.t: This is very effective.
segments.n: ‘Very effective’ says nothing. The answer needs to name a feature in these lines and say what it does, then connect it to Juno.

segments.t: She sees that Dido is in love and that her city has stopped being built, so she goes to talk to Venus.
segments.n: Narrative of lines 90 to 92. Juno’s cunning shows in the language: she is called Saturnia and cara Iovis coniunx, and talibus adgreditur, ‘she approaches with such words’, uses a verb that can mean ‘attack’.

segments.t: She calls Venus’ victory
egregiam vero laudem
‘truly outstanding praise’
which is sarcasm
and this shows she is cunning.
segments.n: The link is asserted. Explain it: by mockingly praising egregiam … laudem et spolia ampla, ‘outstanding glory and rich spoils’, for defeating one woman, Juno shames Venus before offering her deal.

segments.t: dolo
segments.n: dolo on its own loses the sneer. una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est, ‘if one woman has been beaten by the trickery of two gods’, sets una femina against duorum divum to make Venus’ victory look contemptible.

segments.t: means ‘trick’,
which shows that Venus and Cupid tricked Dido.
femina
segments.n: Another single word. The power of femina comes from its place in the line, framed by una … victa, so the weakness of the victim is stressed.

segments.t: means ‘woman’,
which shows that women in the Aeneid are often weak and controlled by the gods, like Dido and Creusa.
segments.n: A generalisation about the whole poem. In this line femina is part of Juno’s taunt, and that is what shows her cunning.

segments.t: Juno then says that she knows Venus is suspicious of Carthage, and asks how long they will keep arguing.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 96 to 98. nec me adeo fallit, ‘nor am I so deceived’, shows Juno pretending frankness to win trust, which is exactly the cunning the question asks about.

segments.t: sed quis erit modus
‘but what will be the limit?’
is a rhetorical question,
segments.n: Naming the rhetorical question is a start; the effect still needs explaining.

segments.t: which makes it persuasive.
segments.n: Say how. The question makes Juno sound reasonable, as if she wants to end a quarrel, which disguises the scheme she is about to propose.

segments.t: Virgil says that Juno saw that Dido was held by such a plague and that her reputation was no longer stopping her madness, and then she spoke to Venus.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 90 to 92. tali … peste teneri, ‘held by such a plague’, presents love as a disease, and Juno is introduced as cara Iovis coniunx and Saturnia, titles that give her weight before she speaks.

segments.t: Juno and Venus are always arguing in the Aeneid. In Book 1 Juno caused the storm that wrecked Aeneas’ ships, and Venus complained to Jupiter, who told her that Aeneas would reach Italy.
segments.n: Book 1 is outside the passage. The question needs evidence of Juno’s cunning in this speech.

segments.t: This shows that Juno is a very cunning goddess.
segments.n: Nothing in the paragraph has been analysed, so the claim is unsupported.

segments.t: In conclusion, Juno is cunning and persuasive because she uses sarcasm and tricks Venus, and she wants to stop Aeneas going to Italy.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the top of the level. It is a fair length, but much of it is narrative paraphrase or background (the judgement of Paris, Juno’s love of Carthage, women in the Aeneid) that does not answer the question. There are two genuine partial points: egregiam vero laudem is quoted, translated and rightly identified as sarcasm, and sed quis erit modus is recognised as a rhetorical question. Neither is developed: the answer asserts that they show cunning and persuasion without explaining how. dolo and femina are picked out as single words, missing the scornful contrast of una … femina and duorum divum. The conclusion restates the question.

exemplars.question: E11a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: This passage is a dramatic turning point because, in a few lines, Dido decides to die, and the story then cuts abruptly to Aeneas, who is about to be driven away by a god.
Dido ends her night of agony with
quin morere ut merita es, ferroque averte dolorem
‘no, die as you deserve, and end your pain with the sword’
The blunt imperative morere, addressed to herself,
makes her pass sentence on herself; merita es shows she believes she deserves it, and ferro makes the method brutally clear.
The decision on which the rest of the book turns is made in a single line.
She then turns on Anna:
tu lacrimis evicta meis, tu prima furentem his, germana, malis oneras atque obicis hosti
‘you, overcome by my tears, you were the first to load me, raging, with these evils, sister, and throw me to the enemy’
The anaphora of tu

points an accusing finger at her sister. The tender word germana is trapped between the violent verbs oneras and obicis, so love and blame are mixed together, and Aeneas, once her guest, is now hosti, an enemy.
Her feelings have turned completely, which makes the moment dramatic.
non licuit thalami expertem sine crimine vitam degere more ferae
‘I was not allowed to live my life without marriage and without blame, like a wild creature’
The comparison more ferae
shows her longing for a simple, innocent life she can never now recover.
The speech closes on
non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo
‘the faith promised to the ashes of Sychaeus has not been kept’
The second non sentence ends on the name Sychaeo,
so her guilt for the broken vow is the last thing she says: her decision to die is also a punishment for betraying her husband.
tantos illa suo rumpebat pectore questus
‘such great laments was she bursting from her heart’
The violent verb rumpebat and the hyperbole tantos
present her grief as something that breaks out of her body, a climax before the sudden change of scene.
Virgil then cuts abruptly to Aeneas:
Aeneas celsa in puppi iam certus eundi carpebat somnos rebus iam rite paratis
‘Aeneas, high on the stern, now certain to go, was snatching sleep, with everything now duly prepared’
The repeated iam and the word rite make him calm and orderly, sleeping while Dido rages.
The contrast between the two lovers at the same moment is stark, and makes us feel the gulf between them at the turning point of the book.
Then
huic se forma dei vultu redeuntis eodem obtulit in somnis
‘to him the shape of the god, returning with the same face, appeared in his sleep’
The sudden vision
marks a second turn: just as Dido chooses death, the gods intervene again to hurry Aeneas away.
omnia Mercurio similis, vocemque coloremque et crines flavos et membra decora iuventae
‘like Mercury in every way, in voice and colouring and golden hair and the graceful limbs of youth’
The polysyndeton, with line 558 ending on a hypermetric -que that runs into the next line,
lingers over the god’s appearance and delays his message,
so the passage ends in suspense, waiting for the warning that will set the departure in motion.

exemplars.commentary: This is an excellent response (Level 5, full marks). It engages with ‘dramatic turning point’ throughout and sees that the passage turns twice, first with Dido’s decision and then with the god’s return. A wide range of precisely selected quotations covers the whole passage, all accurately translated. The analysis is perceptive: germana trapped between the violent verbs, the speech ending on Sychaeo, and the calm of iam and rite set against rumpebat are all developed and linked to the question, and the hypermetric line is correctly identified and tied to the suspense of the ending. More could be said about more ferae, but this is as much as can be expected in the time, and it fully meets the Level 5 descriptor.

exemplars.question: E11a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil makes this a dramatic turning point because Dido decides to kill herself.
quin morere ut merita es
‘rather, die as you deserve’
is an imperative
in which Dido gives an order to herself, which is shocking because she is the queen and is condemning herself to death.
tu lacrimis evicta meis, tu prima furentem
‘you, overcome by my tears, you first, when I was raging’
uses anaphora of tu
to show Dido blaming Anna for persuading her to love Aeneas.
obicis hosti
‘you throw me to the enemy’
shows that she now sees Aeneas as an enemy instead of a lover, which is a big change.
non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo
‘the promise made to the ashes of Sychaeus was not kept’
shows that she feels guilty about breaking her vow to her dead husband.
There is a sudden change of scene to Aeneas:
Aeneas celsa in puppi iam certus eundi
‘Aeneas on the high stern, now certain of going’
He is calm and asleep, which contrasts with Dido, who is in despair,
making the scene more dramatic.

Aeneas has been criticised by many readers for leaving Dido like this, because he does not even say goodbye. However, he is following the orders of the gods, and his duty to found Rome is more important than his love.
segments.n: A general judgement on Aeneas’ character. It does not show how Virgil makes this passage a dramatic turning point.

segments.t: tantos illa suo rumpebat pectore questus
‘such great laments she was pouring out from her heart’
shows how upset Dido is,
which is very dramatic.
segments.n: rumpebat means ‘she was bursting out’: the violent verb makes her grief break out of her body, a climax just before Virgil cuts to the calm Aeneas.

segments.t: Then Mercury appears to Aeneas in a dream, looking the same as before, with his golden hair and young limbs.
segments.n: A retelling of lines 556 to 559. vultu redeuntis eodem, ‘returning with the same face’, and rursus mark a repeat warning, the second push towards departure, which is part of what makes this a turning point.

segments.t: Virgil uses polysyndeton in vocemque coloremque et crines flavos to describe him.
segments.n: Naming polysyndeton is a start. Its effect is to slow the description and linger on the god’s appearance, delaying his message and building suspense; the hypermetric -que at the end of 558 adds to the delay.

segments.t: So this is a turning point because Dido decides to die and Aeneas is told to leave.
This is one of the most famous scenes in Latin literature.
segments.n: A general remark that says nothing about how this passage creates drama.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response in the middle of Level 4. It engages clearly with the question and sees both halves of the passage. The quotations are well chosen and accurately translated, and the anaphora of tu, the change from lover to hosti and the contrast with the calm Aeneas are explained. Development is uneven: the point on Sychaeus is about content only, non licuit … more ferae is not discussed, and rumpebat is quoted but its violence is left as ‘very dramatic’. A paragraph defending Aeneas moves away from the passage. The final section narrates the dream and names polysyndeton without explaining its effect, which is to delay the god’s message and build suspense. The conclusion is sound but restates the opening.

exemplars.question: E11a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: This passage is a dramatic turning point because Dido decides to die and Aeneas decides to leave.

Before this passage Aeneas has been told by Mercury to leave Carthage, and he has argued with Dido, who called him a traitor. Dido has also built a pyre, pretending that it is for a magic ritual to cure her of her love.
segments.n: This summarises earlier events in the book. It may set the scene, but it does not show how Virgil makes these lines a dramatic turning point.

segments.t: In this passage Dido is very upset and says that she should die. She blames her sister Anna for making her fall in love with Aeneas, and says that she has broken her promise to Sychaeus.
segments.n: Paraphrase of Dido’s speech. The drama lies in the Latin: the accusing anaphora tu … tu at Anna, and non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo, ending her speech on her guilt.

segments.t: ferro
segments.n: ferro on its own only means ‘sword’. In ferroque averte dolorem, ‘and end your pain with the sword’, it shows Dido already choosing the means of her death.

segments.t: means ‘sword’,
which is dramatic.
segments.n: Calling a word ‘dramatic’ repeats the question. Explain what the sword adds: the decision to die is now concrete and violent.

segments.t: quin morere ut merita es
‘no, die as you deserve’
shows that Dido thinks she deserves to die,
which is dramatic.
ferae
segments.n: A single word, and misread. The phrase degere more ferae, ‘to live in the manner of a wild creature’, expresses Dido’s wish for a simple, blameless life.

segments.t: means
‘fierce’
segments.n: ferae here is the genitive of fera, ‘a wild animal’, used in the phrase more ferae, ‘like a wild creature’. Taking it as the adjective ‘fierce’ turns Dido’s longing for innocence into anger.

segments.t: which shows how angry Dido is.
segments.n: This conclusion rests on the mistranslation. The phrase shows regret and longing, which makes her decision to die more pitiable.

segments.t: Dido is fierce like an animal because she wants to kill Aeneas.
segments.n: A further wrong point built on the same misreading. In these lines Dido turns her anger on herself and Anna; there is no wish here to kill Aeneas.

segments.t: Meanwhile Aeneas is asleep on his ship because he has got everything ready to leave. Mercury comes to him in a dream again.
segments.n: Narrative of lines 554 to 557. The contrast is the point: Aeneas, iam certus eundi, ‘now certain to go’, carpebat somnos, sleeps calmly while Dido rages, and the abrupt cut is what makes the turning point dramatic.

segments.t: Aeneas is often criticised for leaving Dido, but he has to obey the gods because he is pius and his destiny is to found Rome. Some people think he is cold and heartless, but Virgil shows elsewhere that he is in pain too.
segments.n: A judgement on Aeneas’ character across the book. It does not explain how this passage creates drama.

segments.t: There is a list
segments.n: ‘A list’ needs naming and explaining. It is polysyndeton, which lingers over the god’s appearance and holds back his message.

segments.t: to describe Mercury,
vocemque coloremque et crines flavos
which emphasises what he looks like.
segments.n: Say why that matters: dwelling on his appearance delays the warning and builds suspense, and the hypermetric -que at the end of line 558 runs on into the next line.

segments.t: Dido says that she was not allowed to live her life without marriage and without blame, and that she should not have had these worries.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 550 to 551. The anaphora of non, in non licuit and non servata fides, frames her regrets, and the speech ends on Sychaeo, so her guilt is the last thing she says.

segments.t: There is a lot of emotion in her speech, which makes it dramatic.
segments.n: A general claim with no evidence. Point to a feature, such as the self-address in morere, and explain how it creates drama.

segments.t: Dido is like a tragic heroine because she has a fatal flaw, which is her love for Aeneas, and the audience knows she is going to die.
segments.n: A general comparison with tragedy. It does not explain how these lines become a turning point.

segments.t: In conclusion this is a dramatic turning point because Dido decides to die and Aeneas is told to leave.
After this Dido kills herself on the pyre with Aeneas’ sword, which is the most dramatic part of the book.
segments.n: Her death is outside this passage. The conclusion should draw together how these lines make the turning point dramatic.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), in the middle of the level. It is a reasonable length, but much of it is background from earlier and later in the book or a general defence of Aeneas, and the rest largely narrates the passage. There is one sound point: quin morere ut merita es is quoted, translated and explained as Dido condemning herself. Elsewhere the Latin is single words: ferro is simply called dramatic, and ferae is mistranslated as ‘fierce’, which leads to two wrong points about Dido’s anger and a wish to kill Aeneas. The polysyndeton describing Mercury is quoted but only called ‘a list’. The contrast between the raging Dido and the sleeping Aeneas, the heart of the turning point, is narrated and never analysed.

exemplars.question: E13b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil conveys the force of Dido’s grief and anger by moving from a calm dawn to a violent outburst, first against her own body and then against Aeneas.
et iam prima novo spargebat lumine terras Tithoni croceum linquens Aurora cubile
‘and now early Dawn, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus, was scattering the earth with new light’
This calm, decorative description of dawn in the grand epic style
creates a pause, so her outburst strikes with more force by contrast.
regina e speculis ut primam albescere lucem vidit et aequatis classem procedere velis
‘as soon as the queen from her watchtower saw the first light whitening and the fleet moving off with level sails’
regina reminds us of her status just before she loses all self-control, and the orderly aequatis … velis shows the Trojans leaving calmly.
litoraque et vacuos sensit sine remige portus
‘and she realised the shores and harbours were empty, without an oarsman’
vacuos and sine remige repeat the same idea
to stress the emptiness, the total desertion that drives her grief.
terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum flaventesque abscissa comas
‘striking her beautiful breast three and four times with her hand, and tearing her golden hair’
The phrase terque quaterque and the alliteration of p in pectus percussa
imitate the repeated blows, and the gestures of mourning turn into violence against herself. decorum and flaventes stress her beauty, which makes the self-harm more shocking.
Her grief is physical and intense.
pro Iuppiter! ibit hic
‘O Jupiter! Will this man go?’
The sudden exclamation, with ibit at the end of the line and hic enjambed,
captures her outraged disbelief, and hic, ‘this man’, is contemptuous: she will not even say his name.
nostris inluserit advena regnis?
‘and will a foreigner have made a mockery of my kingdom?’
advena reduces Aeneas to an outsider, and inluserit shows that her pride is hurt.
Her grief has turned to anger.
ite, ferte citi flammas, date tela, impellite remos!
‘go, quickly bring fire, hand out weapons, drive the oars!’
The rush of imperatives in asyndeton
conveys her fury and the speed at which she wants revenge,
so the passage ends at the height of her anger.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response at the bottom of Level 5. It is well organised, tracing the movement from grief to anger and linking it to ‘force’ throughout. Quotations are accurate and well translated, and the contrast with the calm dawn, the alliteration of p, and the enjambment and contempt of hic are developed perceptively. Some points are thinner: the angry rhetorical questions in lines 592 to 593 (non arma expedient …) are not discussed, the final point names asyndeton with only a brief effect, and some quotations are long, with the comment resting on one or two words within them.

exemplars.question: E13b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil shows Dido’s grief and anger in many ways.
At dawn Dido looks out from her watchtower and sees the Trojan fleet sailing away. She sees that the harbour is empty.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 584 to 588. vacuos sensit sine remige portus, ‘she saw the harbours empty, without a rower’, stresses emptiness, and the calm dawn description contrasts with the storm of feeling to come.

segments.t: terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum
‘having struck her lovely breast three and four times with her hand’
shows that she is very upset and is hurting herself.
The numbers three and four emphasise this.
segments.n: terque quaterque is a set phrase for repeated, frantic action; with decorum, ‘lovely’, it shows grief turning violently on her own beauty.

segments.t: terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum
‘striking her beautiful chest three and four times with her hand’
shows that she is very upset, because she is hurting herself.
flaventesque abscissa comas
‘and tearing her golden hair’
also shows her grief.
Dido uses a rhetorical question,
ibit hic
‘will he go?’
to show her anger.
segments.n: Develop it: ibit hic, ‘will he go?’, followed by inluserit advena, ‘will a stranger have mocked’, shows her outrage at being made a fool of, and the dismissive hic refuses even to name him.

segments.t: advena
segments.n: advena alone is just ‘stranger’. In nostris inluserit advena regnis, ‘will a newcomer have mocked our kingdom?’, the word cuts Aeneas down from guest and husband to a mere outsider.

segments.t: means ‘foreigner’,
which shows she now thinks of Aeneas as a stranger.
ite, ferte citi flammas, date tela, impellite remos
‘go, bring flames quickly, give weapons, push the oars’
uses lots of imperatives,
which shows that she wants her people to chase Aeneas,
showing her anger.
Then she asks whether her people will not get their weapons and follow from the whole city, and whether they will not drag the ships out of the dockyards.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 592 to 593. The rhetorical questions non arma expedient … diripientque rates show her anger rising, and diripient, ‘tear away’, is violent.

segments.t: Dido was a strong and successful queen before Aeneas came, and she ruled Carthage well, but now she has lost control because of love.
segments.n: A comment on Dido’s character across the book. The question asks how this passage conveys the force of her feelings.

segments.t: Her anger is also caused by Juno and Venus, who made her fall in love in the first place, so the gods are really to blame.
segments.n: The gods’ part in the story is outside this passage and does not explain Virgil’s language here.

segments.t: In conclusion, Virgil shows that Dido is full of grief and anger because she beats herself and gives orders to chase Aeneas.
Virgil uses lots of techniques to show this.
segments.n: ‘Lots of techniques’ names none. A conclusion should draw together the features already analysed.

segments.t: This is the last time she sees Aeneas, which is very sad.
segments.n: Dido sees the fleet, and sadness at a parting is a different point from how the language conveys the force of her grief and anger.

segments.t: Overall it is a powerful passage which shows exactly how Dido feels about Aeneas leaving.

exemplars.commentary: This is a reasonable response at the bottom of Level 3. It engages with the question and offers relevant quotations, accurately translated. The points, though, stay at the level of content (‘shows that she is very upset’) and say little about how the language conveys the force of her feelings: terque quaterque is said only to emphasise. The opening is narrated, so the contrast between the calm dawn and her outburst is missed, and her rhetorical questions in lines 592 to 593 are retold in English. The rhetorical question ibit hic is named but not explained, advena is a single word without its context, and the imperatives are noted without comment on their speed or asyndeton. Two comments on Dido’s character and the gods drift from the passage, and the conclusion names no technique.

exemplars.question: E13b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil conveys the force of Dido’s grief and anger by showing how upset she is.
Before this, Aeneas has decided to leave secretly in the night after Mercury appeared to him a second time, and Dido has been unable to sleep.
segments.n: Events before the passage. They do not show how Virgil’s language here conveys the force of Dido’s feelings.

segments.t: Aurora
segments.n: A name picked out because it is easy. The dawn lines matter only if their effect is explained: the gentle, colourful croceum … cubile sets a calm scene that Dido’s outburst then shatters.

segments.t: is the goddess of the dawn, who is getting out of bed.
segments.n: This only explains the myth and says nothing about Dido. Link the dawn to the question by contrasting its calm with her grief and anger.

segments.t: Her husband is Tithonus, who was given eternal life but not eternal youth, so he grew older and older.
segments.n: The story of Tithonus is mythological background with no bearing on Dido’s grief or anger.

segments.t: In this passage it is morning and Dido sees the Trojans leaving from her watchtower. She sees that the ships are sailing away and that the harbour is empty.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 586 to 588. vacuos sensit sine remige portus, ‘she saw the harbours empty, without a rower’, stresses emptiness, and that sense of loss is what feeds her grief.

segments.t: She is very sad and angry. She beats her chest three or four times and pulls out her hair.
segments.n: This translates terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum without quoting or analysing it. The repetition terque quaterque and the violence against her own decorum pectus, ‘lovely breast’, show grief turned on herself.

segments.t: This shows her grief.
segments.n: An assertion. The answer needs to say how the details of beating and tearing convey the force of that grief.

segments.t: Then she asks Jupiter if Aeneas is really going to leave, and she tells her people to get weapons and fire and chase after the ships.
segments.n: The whole outburst retold. The force is in the Latin: the exclamation pro Iuppiter!, the scornful hic, and the rapid imperatives ite, ferte, date, impellite.

segments.t: flammas
segments.n: flammas alone shows little. Quoting ferte citi flammas, date tela, impellite remos!, a string of urgent commands in asyndeton, conveys the force of her anger.

segments.t: means ‘flames’,
which foreshadows Dido’s funeral pyre at the end of the book.
segments.n: The pyre comes later and outside the passage. Here the flames are a weapon she orders against the fleet, and that is what shows the force of her anger.

segments.t: She says
nostris inluserit advena regnis
, which means
‘a stranger will have lit up our kingdom’
segments.n: inluserit is from inludo, ‘mock’ or ‘make a fool of’, with nostris … regnis in the dative. Dido is asking whether a newcomer will have mocked her kingdom, which is the source of her rage.

segments.t: which shows that Dido still thinks Aeneas was good for Carthage.
segments.n: This point comes from the mistranslation and reverses the meaning. Dido is furious that Aeneas has made a fool of her and her people.

segments.t: Dido then asks whether her people will not get their weapons and follow from the whole city, and whether others will not tear the ships from the dockyards.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 592 to 593. The rhetorical questions non arma expedient … diripientque rates show her anger rising, and the violent diripient, ‘tear away’, prepares for the commands that follow.

segments.t: She asks lots of questions, which shows she is angry.
segments.n: The questions are not quoted or developed. Explain how their speed and violence convey the force of her anger.

segments.t: Dido was a strong queen who built Carthage herself, so she is used to giving orders, and this is why she gives so many commands here.
segments.n: Her earlier career is background. The commands matter for what they show about her feelings now.

segments.t: In conclusion Virgil conveys the force of Dido’s grief and anger because she is very upset and angry and wants to attack the Trojans.
Later in the book she curses Aeneas and kills herself.
segments.n: Later events add nothing to an answer about how this passage conveys her feelings.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the bottom of the level. Although it is of reasonable length, most of it narrates the passage or adds background: events before the dawn, the myth of Tithonus, and what happens later in the book. Only one Latin phrase is quoted, and inluserit is mistranslated as ‘lit up’ (it means ‘mocked’), which produces a point that reverses Dido’s meaning. Aurora and flammas are picked out as single words. The beating of her breast and the torrent of commands are both described in English without any analysis, so the force of her grief and anger is asserted and never shown from the Latin.

exemplars.question: E15a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Virgil makes Dido’s curse powerful by moving from a terrible fate for Aeneas himself to eternal hatred between two peoples, in solemn, formal language.
si tangere portus infandum caput ac terris adnare necesse est
‘if that unspeakable head must reach harbour and swim to land’
The conditional opening
accepts fate calmly, which makes what follows sound deliberate and controlled, while infandum caput reduces Aeneas to a cursed ‘head’ that she will not name.
at bello audacis populi vexatus et armis, finibus extorris, complexu avulsus Iuli
‘then let him be harassed by the war and arms of a bold people, exiled from his lands, torn from the embrace of Iulus’
The list of participles in asyndeton
heaps one suffering on another. avulsus, ‘torn away’, is especially violent, and choosing his son Iulus makes the curse cruelly personal.
auxilium imploret videatque indigna suorum funera
‘let him beg for help and see the undeserved deaths of his people’
The subjunctives turn wishes into commands, and funera is held over to the start of the next line,
so the word ‘deaths’ lands with heavy force.
sed cadat ante diem mediaque inhumatus harena
‘but let him fall before his time and lie unburied in the middle of the sand’
The climax is an early death and an unburied body, the worst disgrace, so the curse on Aeneas ends at its most terrible.
haec precor, hanc vocem extremam cum sanguine fundo
‘this I pray, this last cry I pour out with my blood’
The polyptoton haec … hanc and the verb fundo, used of pouring an offering,
make her words a sacred offering sealed with her own blood.
nullus amor populis nec foedera sunto
‘let there be no love and no treaties between the peoples’
The legal imperative sunto
makes this sound like a law, so the hatred becomes permanent.
litora litoribus contraria, fluctibus undas imprecor, arma armis
‘I pray for shores against shores, waves against waters, arms against arms’
The polyptoton of litora litoribus and arma armis
sets word against word, acting out the clash between the two nations,
so the curse ends with endless war.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response at the top of Level 4. It engages well with ‘powerful’, has a clear structure that follows the curse from Aeneas to the two peoples, and quotes widely and accurately. The jussive subjunctives, the enjambment of funera, the legal sunto and the polyptoton at the end are well explained. The development is not consistently very good: the point on cadat ante diem … harena describes the content without discussing the language, and the call for an avenger (exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor), perhaps the most powerful moment of the curse, is left out. With those, this would reach Level 5.

exemplars.question: E15a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Dido’s curse is powerful because she wishes terrible things on Aeneas and his people.
infandum caput
‘unspeakable head’
shows how much she hates Aeneas, because she does not even call him by his name.
She prays that he will be attacked in war, driven out of his land and separated from his son, and that he will see his people die.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 615 to 618. The Latin piles up the sufferings in a series of participles, vexatus, extorris, avulsus, and the violent avulsus, ‘torn away’, makes the separation from Iulus brutal.

segments.t: complexu avulsus Iuli
‘torn from the embrace of Iulus’
uses a violent verb,
which makes the curse more painful because it involves his son.
It is very sad that Dido wants this, because she was once a kind queen who welcomed the Trojans.
segments.n: A comment on Dido’s character. The question asks what makes the curse powerful in Virgil’s language.

segments.t: sed cadat ante diem mediaque inhumatus harena
‘but let him die before his time and unburied in the middle of the sand’
is the worst part of the curse, because being unburied was terrible.
She then uses apostrophe,
tum vos, o Tyrii
‘then you, o Tyrians’
to tell her people to hate the Trojans for ever.
exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor
‘may some avenger rise from my bones’
is powerful because she is calling for someone in the future to take revenge.
She tells the Tyrians to hate the Trojans and their descendants for ever, and to send this as a gift to her ashes.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 622 to 624. Asking for hatred as the funeral gift, cinerique haec mittite nostro munera, twists a ritual of love into a curse.

segments.t: Dido’s curse is very important for Roman history because it explains why Rome and Carthage fought the Punic Wars. Hannibal, who is the avenger, nearly destroyed Rome, but in the end the Romans won.
segments.n: History from outside the poem. The question asks how Virgil’s language makes the curse powerful, which the Punic Wars cannot show.

segments.t: haec precor
‘these things I pray’
shows that she is praying to the gods,
which makes the curse serious.
segments.n: The solemn language of prayer, haec precor, hanc vocem extremam cum sanguine fundo, makes the curse a ritual act and her dying words, and that is why it carries such weight.

segments.t: arma armis
‘arms against arms’
is polyptoton
which makes the curse more powerful.
segments.n: Explain how. arma armis sets weapons directly against weapons, so the words themselves clash, and the line pictures endless war between the two peoples.

segments.t: In conclusion, Dido’s curse is powerful because she wants Aeneas to suffer and she wants her people to hate the Trojans for ever.
Virgil uses many devices, which makes it even more powerful.
segments.n: No device is named. A conclusion should pull together the features already discussed, such as the participles and the polyptoton.

exemplars.commentary: This is a reasonable response at the top of Level 3. It engages with the question and covers the whole curse, with accurate quotation and translation. The points on infandum caput and the violent avulsus are sensible, and the avenger is noticed. Development is uneven, though: the list of sufferings and the call for hatred as a funeral gift are retold, haec precor is quoted but only said to make the curse ‘serious’, and the polyptoton at the end is named without saying what it does. The solemn legal force of sunto is missed, and a paragraph on the Punic Wars brings in history from outside the poem. The answer stays on what Dido wishes more than on how Virgil’s language makes it powerful.

exemplars.question: E15a
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Dido’s curse is powerful because she is very angry with Aeneas.
Aeneas has just left Carthage without saying goodbye, after Mercury told him to go, and Dido has realised that she cannot stop him. She is on top of the pyre and is about to kill herself.
segments.n: Background, and partly inaccurate: she climbs the pyre only after the curse. None of it shows how Virgil makes the curse powerful.

segments.t: She says that if Aeneas has to reach Italy then he should suffer in a war and lose his son and see his friends die. She says he should die early and not be buried.
segments.n: A summary of the curse. The power is in the Latin: the participles vexatus, extorris, avulsus pile up his sufferings, and cadat ante diem mediaque inhumatus harena ends on the horror of an unburied body.

segments.t: She calls him
infandum caput
‘unspeakable head’
which shows how much she hates him, because she will not even say his name.
sanguine
segments.n: sanguine on its own is just ‘blood’. hanc vocem extremam cum sanguine fundo, ‘I pour out this last cry with my blood’, makes the curse her dying words, which gives it solemn force.

segments.t: means ‘blood’,
which shows that she is about to die.
nullus amor populis nec foedera sunto
means
‘there is no love for the people and no treaties’
segments.n: sunto is a third person plural imperative: ‘let there be no love between the peoples, nor treaties’. As a command it is a solemn, legal decree, which is where the curse gets its power.

segments.t: which shows she does not want the Carthaginians and the Trojans to be friends.

This curse comes true later in history in the Punic Wars between Rome and Carthage, and Hannibal was the avenger. Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and defeated the Romans at Cannae, but in the end Rome won and destroyed Carthage in 146 BC.
segments.n: The history may be true, but it does not show how Virgil’s language makes the curse powerful. Analyse the Latin, such as exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor, ‘arise, some avenger, from my bones’.

segments.t: There is lots of repetition at the end,
segments.n: Name and explain it. litora litoribus contraria, fluctibus undas … arma armis uses polyptoton to set shore against shore and arms against arms, so the words enact the endless conflict she prays for.

segments.t: like
arma armis
which makes it powerful.
Virgil also uses lots of imperatives, which makes it powerful as well.
segments.n: No imperatives are quoted and their effect is not explained. exercete odiis and mittite, commands to her people, turn a personal grief into a duty of hatred passed down the generations.

segments.t: Then she tells the Tyrians to hate the Trojans and all their descendants for ever, and she says that this should be the gift they give to her ashes.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 622 to 624. exercete odiis and cinerique haec mittite nostro munera turn hatred into the funeral offering she asks for, a chilling idea worth analysing.

segments.t: This is a very dark idea and makes the curse powerful.
segments.n: ‘Very dark’ needs explaining: gifts at a tomb were acts of love and respect, so asking for hatred instead twists a funeral custom into a curse.

segments.t: She also prays that an avenger will rise from her bones and chase the Trojans with fire and sword, now and in the future.
segments.n: Paraphrase of lines 625 to 627. exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor addresses the unborn avenger directly in the second person, and nunc, olim, quocumque … tempore stretches the curse across all time.

segments.t: In conclusion, Dido’s curse is powerful because she is angry and wants revenge on Aeneas and the Trojans for ever.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the top of the level. It is a fair length, but a large part is narrative summary or history from outside the poem (the Punic Wars, Hannibal, the fall of Carthage), and the opening background is partly inaccurate. There are two partial points: infandum caput is quoted, translated and given a plausible effect, and the hostility between the peoples is recognised. However, nullus amor populis nec foedera sunto is mistranslated as a statement when sunto is a command, which misses its solemn force. sanguine is picked out as a single word, and the repetition of arma armis and the imperatives are named but never explained.

drills.question: E6a
drills.weak: uritur means ‘she burns’, which shows Dido is in love.
drills.strong: Virgil opens the line with uritur infelix Dido, ‘unhappy Dido burns’: placing the verb first makes the burning the first thing we hear, and the fire metaphor shows her love consuming her from within, so the picture of her love is vivid and painful.
drills.why: The weak point picks out one word and translates it. The stronger one quotes the whole phrase, names the metaphor and the word order, and explains what they show about her love.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.68–79: In this passage, how does Virgil make this a vivid picture of Dido’s love for Aeneas?

drills.question: E5a
drills.weak: medullas means ‘marrow’, which shows her love is very deep.
drills.strong: est molles flamma medullas, ‘the flame eats at her soft marrow’: the metaphor of a fire burning into the marrow, the innermost part of the body, shows love devouring her from inside, so the sacrifices she performs on the outside cannot reach it.
drills.why: A single word cannot carry a point. Quoting the phrase lets you name the metaphor and connect it to the question about why her prayers and sacrifices fail.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.56–67: In this passage, how does Virgil show that Dido’s prayers and sacrifices cannot help her?

drills.question: E12a
drills.weak: moras means ‘delays’, which shows Aeneas is delaying.
drills.strong: heia age, rumpe moras, ‘come on, break off your delay’: the brisk interjection heia age and the short, sharp imperative rumpe, a violent verb, make Mercury sound impatient, so the warning ends with an urgent call to act at once.
drills.why: The weak point translates one word and states the obvious. The stronger one quotes the whole command and explains how its sound and its verb create urgency.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.560–570: In this passage, how does Virgil make Mercury’s warning urgent?

drills.question: E4b
drills.latin: his dictis impenso animum flammavit amore spemque dedit dubiae menti solvitque pudorem
drills.weak: After Anna’s speech Dido is even more in love, she has more hope, and she no longer feels ashamed.
drills.strong: his dictis impenso animum flammavit amore spemque dedit dubiae menti solvitque pudorem, ‘with these words she set her heart ablaze with boundless love, gave hope to her wavering mind and loosened her sense of shame’: the tricolon of verbs (flammavit, dedit, solvit) shows Anna’s words working step by step, and solvit pudorem, placed last, marks the final barrier giving way, so we see her resistance overcome.
drills.why: The weak point retells what happens. The stronger one quotes the Latin and shows how the structure of the sentence enacts Dido’s resistance breaking down.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.47–55: In this passage, how does Virgil show Anna’s words overcoming Dido’s resistance?

drills.question: E14a
drills.latin: non potui abreptum divellere corpus et undis spargere
drills.weak: Dido wishes she had torn Aeneas’ body apart and thrown it into the sea, and killed his men and Ascanius.
drills.strong: non potui abreptum divellere corpus et undis spargere? ‘could I not have seized his body, torn it apart and scattered it on the waves?’: the rhetorical question shows her regretting violence she did not commit, and the run of violent verbs (abreptum, divellere, spargere), with spargere enjambed to the start of the next line, makes the imagined attack savage, which conveys the force of her anger.
drills.why: Retelling the content shows understanding but earns little. The stronger point quotes the Latin and explains how the question form, the verbs and the enjambment convey the force of her anger.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.595–606: In this passage, how does Virgil convey the force of Dido’s anger?

drills.question: E9b
drills.latin: speluncam Dido dux et Troianus eandem devenient
drills.weak: Juno says that Dido and Aeneas will go into the same cave, and then she will marry them.
drills.strong: speluncam Dido dux et Troianus eandem devenient, ‘Dido and the Trojan leader will come to the same cave’: speluncam … eandem frames the two names, so the word order shuts the lovers inside the cave together, and devenient, held over to the next line, makes their meeting sound fixed and inevitable, an ominous sign that the ‘wedding’ is a trap.
drills.why: The weak point paraphrases Juno’s plan. The stronger one looks at the word order and the placing of the verb, and links them to ‘ominous’.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.120–128: In this passage, how does Virgil make Juno’s account of the storm and the ‘wedding’ ominous?

drills.question: E6a
drills.weak: Virgil uses a simile comparing Dido to a deer.
drills.strong: qualis coniecta cerva sagitta, ‘like a deer struck by an arrow’: the simile makes Dido the wounded animal and Aeneas the shepherd who shot her without knowing it (nescius), and haeret lateri letalis harundo, ‘the deadly arrow sticks in her side’, shows that she cannot escape her love however far she runs, so the picture is both vivid and doomed.
drills.why: Naming a simile earns nothing on its own. The stronger point explains what each part of the comparison stands for and why that makes her love vivid.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.68–79: In this passage, how does Virgil make this a vivid picture of Dido’s love for Aeneas?

drills.question: E2b
drills.weak: There is alliteration of v in veteris vestigia, which is effective.
drills.strong: agnosco veteris vestigia flammae, ‘I recognise the traces of the old flame’: the soft alliteration of v slows the line into a confession, and the metaphor of a flame rekindled shows that the love she once felt for Sychaeus has returned for Aeneas, so the oath that follows is powerful because it is sworn against a feeling she has already admitted.
drills.why: ‘Effective’ is not an effect. The stronger point says what the sound and the metaphor do, and ties them to the power of the oath.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.20–30: In this passage, how does Virgil make Dido’s oath of loyalty to Sychaeus powerful?

drills.question: E12a
drills.weak: This is a generalisation about women, which emphasises the point.
drills.strong: varium et mutabile semper femina, ‘a woman is always a fickle and changeable thing’: the neuter adjectives varium et mutabile reduce Dido to a ‘thing’, and femina, held over to the start of the next line, lands as a blunt final word, so Mercury frightens Aeneas into leaving at once.
drills.why: The weak point identifies the feature and stops. The stronger one explains the grammar and the placing of femina, and links them to the urgency of the warning.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.560–570: In this passage, how does Virgil make Mercury’s warning urgent?

drills.question: E5a
drills.latin: heu, vatum ignarae mentes! quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant?
drills.weak: Sacrifices were very important in Roman religion, so Virgil’s readers would have respected Dido for making them.
drills.strong: heu, vatum ignarae mentes! quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant? ‘ah, the ignorant minds of seers! what use are prayers, what use are shrines, to a woman who is raging?’: the narrator’s exclamation and the anaphora of quid in the rhetorical questions tell us directly that the rituals are useless, and furentem shows that her madness is beyond their reach.
drills.why: Background on Roman religion does not answer how Virgil shows that her prayers cannot help. The stronger point stays with the passage, where the narrator says so himself.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.56–67: In this passage, how does Virgil show that Dido’s prayers and sacrifices cannot help her?

drills.question: E14a
drills.latin: quem secum patrios aiunt portare penates, quem subiisse umeris confectum aetate parentem
drills.weak: Aeneas is famous for his pietas, and in Book 2 he carries his father out of Troy, which shows he is a good son.
drills.strong: quem secum patrios aiunt portare penates, quem subiisse umeris confectum aetate parentem, ‘the man who, they say, carries his ancestral gods with him, who carried his father, worn out with age, on his shoulders’: the anaphora of quem and the sneering aiunt, ‘they say’, turn Aeneas’ famous devotion into a story she no longer believes, so her bitter sarcasm shows the force of her anger.
drills.why: The weak point praises Aeneas, which is the opposite of what Dido is doing. The question is about her anger, so the stronger point shows how she mocks his reputation.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.595–606: In this passage, how does Virgil convey the force of Dido’s anger?

drills.question: E10a
drills.weak: rursusne procos inrisa priores experiar means ‘shall I laugh at my old suitors again?’, which shows Dido is proud.
drills.strong: rursusne procos inrisa priores experiar, ‘am I, a laughing-stock, to try my former suitors again?’: inrisa is passive, so Dido imagines herself as the one mocked, and the deliberative question shows her humiliation as she looks for a way out, which makes her despair vivid.
drills.why: inrisa is a perfect passive participle describing Dido: she is the one laughed at. Misreading it turns her humiliation into pride and reverses the point.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.529–546: In this passage, how does Virgil make Dido’s despair vivid?

drills.question: E2b
drills.weak: ille habeat secum servetque sepulcro means ‘he has it with him and serves it in the tomb’, which shows Sychaeus is dead.
drills.strong: ille habeat secum servetque sepulcro, ‘let him keep it with him and guard it in his grave’: the jussive subjunctives habeat and servet make this a solemn command, and the alliteration of s in secum servetque sepulcro gives a hushed, final tone, so her love is sealed in the tomb with Sychaeus and the oath sounds absolute.
drills.why: habeat and servet are subjunctives expressing a wish or command, and servare means ‘keep’ or ‘guard’. Getting them right reveals the solemnity that makes the oath powerful.
drills.context: Virgil, Aeneid IV.20–30: In this passage, how does Virgil make Dido’s oath of loyalty to Sychaeus powerful?

comments.text: Centres have become more aware of the need for developed analysis in 15-mark response questions: quoting a meaningful portion of Latin, then translating and discussing it in order to answer the question.
For 15-mark questions, candidates should be encouraged to quote and translate whole Latin phrases.
In some rare cases, the entire response was limited by having no reference at all to the Latin texts.
Fragmentary approaches which zone in on isolated words are unlikely to be credited.
focused too much on single isolated words, or words with English translations of Latin words which were easily recognisable (e.g. equus Troianus)
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: produced undeveloped analysis in 15-mark responses, often retelling the narrative with English paraphrases, or picking out isolated words with obvious English derivations but which did not show knowledge of their context in the passage
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: The most successful responses were able to capture the drama in this scene rather than simply narrating what happened in a linear progression through the passage.

While many scripts were extremely impressive, it was noticeable that a sizeable number were very narrative-heavy in their approaches. These responses tended to repeat the narrative of the text with some analysis of particular word choices but often neglecting the rich literary features that the texts contained.
In some cases, there was also a tendency to simply go through the narration of the passage to show how interesting it was. Greater levels of (stylistic) analysis would help prevent this shortcoming.
produced insightful responses to 15-mark questions by providing relevant evidence from the Latin texts and detailed discussion of relevant literary devices
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: contained detailed discussion of relevant literary devices, both identifying these features and explaining their effects well
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: Literary features can then be further analysed, and their relevance carefully explained.
Knowledge of the style of authors was also in evidence, though at times the development of these points could be stronger in order to point out the effects of such devices.
did not appreciate or evaluate the wealth of literary and rhetorical devices
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: Several candidates seemed to find the use of litotes at times when an author made a negation. It should be noted that litotes is a literary device in which an author uses an understatement (often through mentioning the negative of a positive quality) which has the effect of adding an ironic tone or downplaying some fact.
Candidates were able to identify a range of emotions from outrage to sorrow and indignation, all of which were explained with well-selected evidence.
15-mark responses were focused on the question being asked, e.g. how the passage is ‘dramatic’, etc.
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: Both content and use of language should be linked to the original question – e.g. how is a passage lively, or vivid, or how does it show an impressive character?
A piece of literary style is identified and discussed, before the whole point is clearly linked back to the question.

A range of points should be taken from the whole passage: sometimes, candidates offer perhaps multiple points of analysis on the same Latin quote which restricts the attention they give to other parts of the passage.

As often happens, a few candidates spent too much time on the 15-mark questions and ended up having to finish the 20-mark essay abruptly. The importance of good timing should be noted again by all centres.
It is always worth asking: are candidates spending too much time on the 15-mark questions?
There is ample quotation of Latin which is embedded in the context of the overall narrative.
